name: Wendy Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play ukulele at community events, record simple chord guides and help an experienced tutor teach adult beginners. I kept accounts for a small shop before changing work at 54. I finished secondary school and I can count fees accurately, but I am still learning how to teach an awkward chord.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that mean for home now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner and I have grown children, a mortgage and eight months of expenses saved. Bookings are good enough to pay above the usual musician rate; I have not yet checked a pension estimate, so I count booked fees instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the events manager that a quicker booking list is useful if every player’s fee remains visible. I would still bring an instrument and listen to the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our eight-month reserve and current paid bookings cover an ordinary cancellation. There are plenty of other events nearby, so the mortgage feels manageable this term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This season I would keep the paid ukulele events, chord guides and supervised adult lessons. I use AI occasionally for a first event note, but I check names, prices and dates against the signed booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm about this picture. There is no reason to turn a little paperwork into a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What fee term would you check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a written cancellation fee before accepting the next festival date. A booking without a written cancellation fee is harder to rely on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you checked retirement income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. I would request a written estimate this winter and keep the paid events while I read it.

I would keep **live ukulele playing** at events.
think: Our **eight-month reserve** covers an ordinary cancellation without making the household mortgage payment uncertain.
Plenty of **nearby bookings** keep current income secure.
do: Keep **paid events**, chord guides and supervised lessons this season.
Request a **written cancellation fee** before the next festival date.
Request a **written retirement estimate** this winter while keeping paid events.
feel: I feel **calm** about current bookings and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the event manager that AI can make a chord guide cheaply, but an adult still needs a paid teacher to adjust a hand. I would ask which lesson and preparation hours are in the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guide recordings are about a quarter of my own pay, and some organisers might choose generated ones. I could look for more events, but a lost quarter would still change our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would request written paid lesson and preparation hours and a paid tutor-led lesson on the centre’s new chord checker. In the first year I would test it only on my own nameless guide if the centre approves local storage; I would play every suggested chord against the original and stop if a change is wrong or the file leaves the centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about losing guide fees. The reserve buys time, not a licence to work without pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you feed a learner’s recording into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would keep the learner’s name and voice in the centre folder; my own guide is enough for a trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply for another event role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If paid guides or lessons actually fall, I would apply for a posted paid community-music assistant job only if my secondary schooling and supervised experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces the lost fees and the bus home works; I would keep current events until a signed offer. A job title alone would not replace the lost guide income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the organisers that AGI by 2028 could print and play a chord guide in seconds. I would ask them to sign the paid live dates before the calendar fills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the guide sales to end in 2028, but families still pay for someone to correct a real chord. Robots that can handle instruments arrive around 2031, three years later. My paid chord-guide recording work could disappear before robots play instruments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total guide invoices and request signed paid event dates. In the first year after 2028, if paid lesson or event hours also fall, I would apply for a posted adult-music aide role only if my schooling and supervised experience qualify, written net pay after travel covers lost fees and the last bus works; I would keep current events and pupils until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the lost guide quarter. Eight months saved and many local events give me room to search if paid hours also fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new instrument now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a signed paid event covers its cost. I would leave six months of household expenses untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 60 in 2028, but I have not checked any pension amount. I would request a written estimate and keep earning while I read it.

I would tell organisers **AGI** can make chord guides quickly.

S2.quote: My paid chord-guide recording work could disappear before robots play instruments.
fieldNote: Her **2028 guide loss** precedes capable playing robots around 2031.
The **aide move** needs actual paid-hour cuts, qualified posted work, written net pay, bus and signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the centre that five years until AGI by 2031 is time to see whether adults will pay for a proper beginner group. I would still have the experienced tutor lead the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect guide sales to end by 2031, and playing robots could appear around 2034. A paid group could replace fees. A ukulele group full of unpaid helpers is not income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would offer a six-week ukulele group only if the experienced tutor agrees to paid supervision, the centre commits a room and hire cost in writing before deposits, and eight adults prepay enough for room, inspected loan instruments, travel, the tutor’s wage and my teaching and preparation. In the first year after 2031 I would repeat only while eight safe paid places still cover both wages, preparation, room, instruments and travel; if an instrument fails, I would replace it safely or defer and refund the whole group below that floor, keeping existing pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about losing the guide quarter, even while testing a paid block. Our reserve could absorb a cancelled idea, but I would not spend it on the tutor’s fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a loan ukulele is unsafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre technician must check strings and bridges before anyone plays. If a loan ukulele is unsafe, I would find a safe replacement before class; if that leaves fewer than eight safe paid places, I would defer and refund the whole group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only four adults prepay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refund all four and keep the regular lessons. Four fees do not cover two teachers and the room.

I would have an **experienced tutor** lead any group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the centre that a decade until AGI by 2036 lets us agree fair teaching and preparation fees. A long warning is useful only when the paid hours are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guide sales may end by 2036 and playing robots may reach community shows around 2039. We have eight months saved and other local work now, but I need a written view of retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I would request a written pension estimate and save ten percent of each extra paid event fee after mortgage, food and travel, aiming for twelve months while leaving six untouched. In the first year after 2036, if paid event or lesson hours fall, I would apply for a posted arts-centre music aide job only if my schooling qualifies, written net pay after travel covers the losses and bus service works; I would keep current paid events and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about later income changes, not afraid of next month’s bill. A written estimate will help me plan without pretending I know the answer today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no extra fees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I save nothing new that week. Six months of expenses stay untouched rather than becoming tuition money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop work at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 in 2036, but I have set no retirement date. I would look at the estimate and the paid hours still offered.

fieldNote: Her **twelve-month goal** uses extra paid event fees after essentials, protecting six months.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the guides could stop selling before I know whether paid lessons or events will hold. Signed event dates, a real qualified aide opening and a bus home would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the borrowed ukuleles. A child or adult deserves an instrument that works before paying for a lesson.

headlineQuote: A child or adult deserves an instrument that works before paying for a lesson.
portrait: At **58**, Wendy is a junior ukulele player who moved from shop accounts and completed secondary school.
Her higher **musician pay**, eight-month reserve and many local events support near-term security.
She uses **AI occasionally** and tests a new chord checker only with paid instruction, approved storage and manual playing.
A **paid ukulele group** requires an experienced paid tutor, eight prepayments, written room hire, safe instruments and both wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase guide fees before she knows whether paid lessons and events will hold.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed event dates**, a qualified posted aide opening with written net pay and workable bus service would help Wendy.
